To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of the histone-like HUB protein in the cell changes the persistence length and cyclization properties of DNA, and that the local bending and undertwilting of DNA by HUB provide a structural rationale of the condensation of nucleoid and expression of reporter genes in the cell.

(1) the presence of HUS at levels approximating the physiological levels in the cell reduces DNA persistence length by roughly 3-fold compared to that of naked DNA; (2) binding of HU to short duplexes changes their cyclization properties in a way that can not be mimicked by the simple wormlike model of DNA; (3) binding of protein to short duplexes depends on chain length and accumulates on successfully closed chains; and (4) the uptake of HUS
the binding of HU to short DNA segments induces structural distortions of DNA, which reduce its flexibility and alter its cyclization and supercoiling properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of HU on the structural properties of the DNA and the role of the HU in DNA organization in vivo.
the effects of HU on the structural, mechanical, and topological properties of DNA and the implications of these changes for the function of the bacterial nucleoid in vivo.
the effect of the histone-like protein HU on DNA structure, flexibility, ring-closure and supercoiling, which are the basic physical properties of DNA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the HU protein, which is a major constituent of the E. coli nucleoid, has a major impact on the structure, dynamics, and topology of the bacterial genome, with important implications for the regulation of gene expression.
HU binding to the DNA has a profound effect on its structure, flexibility, cyclization, and topology.
HU is an important structural component of the bacterial chromosome that contributes significantly to DNA condensation and the regulation of gene expression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HU binding to the nucleoid DNA induces local deformations of DNA that are sufficient to explain the observed changes in DNA structure, flexibility, cyclization, and supercoiling.
HU is a very flexible protein that can bend DNA in many different ways, but it has a strong preference to bind to the minor groove of DNA and induce a local bend of 40-45 degrees.
HU is not just a simple DNA-binder, but it has a profound impact on the structure of DNA, and this impact is not just a random one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HU binding to short DNA segments is highly heterogeneous, and this heterogeneity is a key factor in the effects that HU binding has on the properties of DNA.
the effects of HU binding cannot be captured by the conventional wormlike model, but must be treated in a more detailed fashion.

the effects of nonsymmetrically bound HU on the biophysical properties of double-helical nucleic acids are much more complex than previously appreciated and cannot be described in terms of a simple wormlike chain.
